We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
Structural and surface agreement signals reliably predict output quality ($\rho$ up to 0.52 on Few-NERD, 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.42 on the primary test bed; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging regardless of selection regime.
However, quality estimation does not translate to structural selection: despite 10--19~pp oracle headroom, no structural signal significantly outperforms greedy decoding on any dataset.
The gap stems from two jointly operating mechanisms: instance degeneracy (21--58\% of instances produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, scaling with model capability) and LP compression (median within-instance range of 0.041 nats).
A LoRA-rank ablation reduces degeneracy from 21\% to 7\% without enabling selection; supervised verifiers combining all five signals (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) fail to close the oracle gap, confirming the bottleneck is in the feature space.
Selection effectiveness is signal-dependent: LP achieves significant gains on Few-NERD ($+1.17$~pp, $p{<}0.05$) where type confusion invalidates structural consensus, while structural signals uniformly degrade.
The gap is regime-dependent (signal collapse at low-resource boundary, marginal structural success at ceiling, LP success in the type-confusion regime) and whether it persists at 70B+ scales remains open.
Closing the structural gap requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; LP provides a lightweight cross-domain baseline where model uncertainty is not compressed.
